items.title: Location, Extent, Regions & Relief
items.body:
**In one line:** This note fixes where Andhra Pradesh (AP) sits on the map, how big it is, how many districts it now has, and the three kinds of land it is made of.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC loves one-mark facts here — area rank, number of districts, the highest peak — and these facts anchor almost every other Geography answer about AP.

## The story

In **2014** the old Andhra Pradesh was split into two states: **Telangana** was carved out, and the remaining part is today's AP. Because of that split, present-day AP sits on India's **south-east coast**, with the **Bay of Bengal** to its east.

By size it covers about **1,62,970 sq km**. After Jammu & Kashmir became a Union Territory in 2019, AP is now the **7th largest** state by area, and the **10th** by population (about 4.09% of India in the 2011 Census).

The number of districts has grown in steps. It was **13** for decades, rose to **26** on **4 April 2022**, and then to **28** on **31 December 2025** when **Polavaram** and **Markapuram** districts were added. A proposed **Madanapalle** district was never created — Madanapalle is only the headquarters town of Annamayya district.

If you look at AP from the sea moving inland, the land changes in three clear belts, and this is its **physiography** (the shape of its surface).

## Picture it

| Belt (west to east) | What it is like |
|---|---|
| Rayalaseema plateau | Dry, semi-arid interior on the edge of the Deccan |
| Eastern Ghats | Broken, low hill ranges (Nallamala, Papikonda, Seshachalam, Erramala) |
| Coastal plains | Flat, fertile east-coast land with the Godavari and Krishna deltas |

The highest point is **Arma Konda (about 1,680 m)** in Alluri Sitharama Raju district — it is also the tallest peak in the whole Eastern Ghats.

## Terms explained

- **Bifurcation** — the 2014 splitting of one state into two (AP and Telangana).
- **Physiography** — the natural shape of the land surface (plains, hills, plateau).
- **Plateau** — a raised, flat-topped area of land; Rayalaseema sits on the Deccan plateau's margin.
- **Delta** — the fan of fertile land a river builds where it meets the sea.
- **Rayalaseema and Coastal Andhra** — AP's two broad regions; the far-north coast (Srikakulam-Vizianagaram-Visakhapatnam), called Uttarandhra, is often treated as a third sub-region.

## Don't confuse

- **Districts 26 versus 28** — older books and the 2024-25 state survey still print 26; the correct current figure is **28** (since 31 Dec 2025).
- **Arma Konda is NOT Mahendragiri** — Mahendragiri is a high Eastern Ghats peak but lies on the Odisha side and is lower.
- **7th not 8th** — AP was the 8th largest state only before 2019, when J&K was still a state.

## Remember it

Count the districts up: **13, then double to 26, then plus 2 (Polavaram and Markapuram) to 28.**

## TL;DR

- AP lies on India's south-east (Bay of Bengal) coast; area about 1,62,970 sq km; 7th largest state, 10th by population.
- Districts grew 13 to 26 (4 Apr 2022) to 28 (31 Dec 2025, Polavaram and Markapuram); Madanapalle is only a headquarters.
- Three belts west to east: Rayalaseema plateau, Eastern Ghats, coastal plains.
- Highest point: Arma Konda (about 1,680 m), the tallest peak of the Eastern Ghats.
keyPoints: AP lies on India's south-east (Bay of Bengal) coast; about 1,62,970 sq km; 7th largest state and 10th by population.
Two regions (Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema); the north-coastal Srikakulam-Vizianagaram-Visakhapatnam belt is a distinct sub-region.
Districts: 13 to 26 (4 April 2022) to 28 with Polavaram and Markapuram (31 December 2025); the 2024-25 survey still shows 26.
Three physiographic belts west to east: Rayalaseema plateau, Eastern Ghats, coastal plains.
Arma Konda (about 1,680 m), in Alluri Sitharama Raju district, is AP's highest point and the tallest Eastern Ghats peak.
items.source: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25; List of districts of Andhra Pradesh (28, verified); Geography of India (Arma Konda 1,690 m)

items.title: Coastline & Ports
items.body:
**In one line:** AP has a long sea edge on the Bay of Bengal, and this coastline is both a money-maker (ports, fishing) and the reason the state is so exposed to cyclones.

**Why it is asked:** The '974 km' figure and the name of AP's only major port (Visakhapatnam) are classic one-mark questions; the coast also links to economy and disaster-management answers.

## The story

A **coastline** is simply the length of the boundary where the land meets the sea. AP's coastline runs about **974 km** along the Bay of Bengal — the **longest of any state on India's east coast**.

The shape of this coast changes as you move along it. In the centre it is low and flat, built up by the mud the **Godavari and Krishna** rivers drop as they reach the sea. In the north, around **Visakhapatnam**, it is rockier, which is why a deep natural harbour could form there.

That natural harbour makes **Visakhapatnam** AP's only **major port** (a 'major' port is one run under the central government). Alongside it, several **non-major ports** — **Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada and Machilipatnam** — handle cargo, fishing boats and industry. Because the coast is so long, AP is also a national leader in **fishing and shrimp farming (aquaculture)**, much of it exported.

## Picture it

| Port | Type |
|---|---|
| Visakhapatnam | Major port (central government); deep natural harbour |
| Krishnapatnam | Non-major port |
| Gangavaram | Non-major port |
| Kakinada | Non-major port |
| Machilipatnam | Non-major port |

## Terms explained

- **Coastline** — the length of the shore where land meets the sea.
- **Major port** — a large port administered by the central government; AP has exactly one (Visakhapatnam).
- **Harbour** — a sheltered stretch of water where ships can anchor safely.
- **Aquaculture** — farming fish or shrimp in ponds or coastal waters, rather than catching them wild.

## Don't confuse

- **Longest on the east coast, not in all India** — Gujarat has India's longest coastline overall; AP's 974 km is the longest on the eastern side.
- **Major versus non-major port** — only Visakhapatnam is 'major'; Kakinada, Krishnapatnam and the rest are non-major, even though they are busy.

## Remember it

'**974** — nine, seven, four' is AP's east-coast score; and its one big port starts with the same sound as the state's biggest city, **V**isakhapatnam.

## TL;DR

- AP's coastline is about 974 km, the longest on India's east coast.
- Visakhapatnam is AP's only major (central-government) port, built on a natural harbour.
- Non-major ports: Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada, Machilipatnam.
- The long coast powers fishing and shrimp aquaculture but also exposes AP to Bay of Bengal cyclones.
keyPoints: AP coastline is about 974 km, the longest on India's east coast.
Visakhapatnam is AP's only major (central-government) port, a deep natural harbour.
Non-major ports: Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada, Machilipatnam.
The coast supports fishing and shrimp aquaculture but is highly cyclone-prone.
items.source: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25; Transport in Andhra Pradesh (974 km, verified)

items.title: Rivers, River-sharing & Irrigation Projects
items.body:
**In one line:** AP's rivers all flow east into the Bay of Bengal, feed its deltas, and are tapped by big dams and lift schemes — most famously Polavaram on the Godavari.

**Why it is asked:** Matching a reservoir to its river (Nagarjuna Sagar to Krishna, Somasila to Pennar, Polavaram to Godavari) is a very common APPSC match-the-following item.

## The story

AP has about **40 rivers** of all sizes, and **15 of them are inter-state** (they are shared with neighbouring states). Every important river flows **eastward into the Bay of Bengal**.

The two giants are the **Godavari** and the **Krishna**. The **Godavari** is the largest river of peninsular India and is nicknamed the **'Dakshina Ganga'** (the Ganga of the South); it builds the lush Konaseema delta. The **Krishna** builds its own delta near Machilipatnam. In the dry south, the **Pennar (Penna)** waters Rayalaseema and Nellore, while in the far north the **Vamsadhara and Nagavali** (shared with Odisha) drain the Srikakulam-Vizianagaram belt.

Because rain is uneven, AP stores and moves river water using **irrigation projects**. A dam creates a **reservoir** (a man-made lake) whose water is let out through canals. The flagship is **Polavaram** on the Godavari, which the centre has made a **National Project**. On the Krishna sit **Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam**; on the Pennar sits **Somasila**. A **lift scheme** called **Handri-Neeva** even pumps Krishna water uphill into drought-hit Rayalaseema.

## Picture it

| Reservoir / project | River | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Polavaram | Godavari | National Project; AP's flagship |
| Nagarjuna Sagar | Krishna | Large multipurpose reservoir |
| Srisailam | Krishna | Hydro-power and irrigation |
| Somasila | Pennar | Serves Nellore / Rayalaseema |
| Handri-Neeva (lift) | Krishna water | Pumped to Rayalaseema |

## Terms explained

- **Inter-state river** — a river shared by more than one state, so its water is divided by agreements or tribunals.
- **Reservoir** — the lake of water held back by a dam.
- **National Project** — a scheme the central government funds and supervises because of its national importance; Polavaram is one.
- **Lift scheme** — a project that pumps water uphill, against gravity, to reach dry higher land.
- **Dakshina Ganga** — 'Ganga of the South', the Godavari's nickname.

## Don't confuse

- **Polavaram is on the Godavari, not the Krishna.** The Krishna carries Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam.
- **Somasila is on the Pennar**, not the Godavari or Krishna.
- **Vamsadhara/Nagavali are shared with Odisha**, while the Krishna and Pennar are shared with Karnataka.

## Remember it

Delta duo = **Godavari + Krishna**; Rayalaseema's lifeline = **Handri-Neeva**.

## TL;DR

- About 40 rivers (15 inter-state); all major rivers drain east into the Bay of Bengal.
- Godavari (largest peninsular river, 'Dakshina Ganga') and Krishna build AP's deltas.
- Polavaram is a National Project on the Godavari; Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam are on the Krishna; Somasila is on the Pennar.
- Handri-Neeva lifts Krishna water to drought-prone Rayalaseema.
keyPoints: AP has about 40 rivers (15 inter-state); all major rivers drain east into the Bay of Bengal.
Godavari (largest peninsular river, 'Dakshina Ganga') is shared with Maharashtra, Odisha, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh and MP.
Krishna is shared with Maharashtra and Karnataka; Pennar with Karnataka; Vamsadhara and Nagavali with Odisha.
Polavaram is a National Project on the Godavari; Nagarjuna Sagar and Srisailam are on the Krishna; Somasila on the Pennar.
Handri-Neeva lifts Krishna water to Rayalaseema.
items.mnemonic: Delta duo = Godavari + Krishna; Rayalaseema lifeline = Handri-Neeva.

figure.caption: Rivers drain east to the Bay of Bengal: Godavari (Polavaram), Krishna (Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam), Pennar (Somasila); Handri-Neeva serves Rayalaseema.

items.title: Climate, Agro-climatic Zones, Soils & Land Use
items.body:
**In one line:** AP's weather splits into a wet, cyclone-hit coast and a dry, drought-prone interior; its soils and land use follow the same split, with crop-growing land taking the biggest share.

**Why it is asked:** The 'six agro-climatic zones', the name of the drought zone, and 'which soil in the delta' are frequent one-mark questions.

## The story

AP's **climate** is broadly **tropical** (hot). But it is not the same everywhere. The **coast** is hot, humid and among India's **most cyclone-prone** areas, because Bay of Bengal storms hit it. **Rayalaseema**, especially **Anantapuramu**, is **semi-arid and drought-prone** — one of the driest tracts in India.

Most rain comes from the **south-west monsoon** (June to September). Unusually, the **south coast** also gets useful rain from the **north-east (retreating) monsoon** (October to December), when winds reverse and blow back out over the sea.

To plan farming, AP is divided into **six agro-climatic zones** — areas grouped by their climate and soil. The dry Kurnool and Anantapuramu tract is the **Scarce Rainfall Zone**.

**Soil** is the loose top layer plants grow in. The rich **deltaic alluvial** soil of the Godavari-Krishna deltas grows paddy; **black cotton (regur)** soil covers the Deccan and Rayalaseema; **red loamy and sandy** soils fill the interior.

Finally, **land use** describes how the state's total area is used. Crop land (**net area sown**) takes the single biggest share.

## Picture it

| Land-use category (2023-24) | Share |
|---|---|
| Net area sown | about 30.4% |
| Recorded forest | about 22.63% |
| Current fallows | about 14.9% |
| Non-agricultural use | about 12.84% |
| Barren / uncultivable | about 8.19% |

## Terms explained

- **Tropical climate** — a hot climate with no true cold season.
- **Semi-arid** — dry, with low and unreliable rainfall, but not a full desert.
- **Agro-climatic zone** — a region grouped by its climate and soil for farm planning; AP has six.
- **Alluvial soil** — fertile soil made of silt a river deposits.
- **Net area sown** — the land actually under crops in a year (the biggest land use in AP).
- **Current fallow** — farm land left unsown for a season to recover.

## Don't confuse

- **South-west versus north-east monsoon** — the south-west (June-September) gives most of AP's rain; the north-east (October-December) adds extra rain mainly on the south coast.
- **Six zones, not five or seven** — the drought one is the Scarce Rainfall Zone (Kurnool + Anantapuramu).

## Remember it

Coast = **wet and stormy**; Rayalaseema = **dry and thirsty**; crop land wins the land-use share.

## TL;DR

- Climate is tropical: a cyclone-prone humid coast versus a semi-arid, drought-prone Rayalaseema (Anantapuramu is driest).
- Most rain is from the south-west monsoon; the south coast also gains north-east (retreating) monsoon rain.
- Six agro-climatic zones; the Scarce Rainfall Zone is Kurnool + Anantapuramu.
- Main soils: deltaic alluvial, black cotton (regur) and red loamy/sandy; net area sown (about 30.4%) is the largest land use.
keyPoints: AP climate is tropical: cyclone-prone humid coast versus semi-arid, drought-prone Rayalaseema (Anantapuramu driest).
South coastal districts also gain rain from the north-east (retreating) monsoon.
Six agro-climatic zones; the Scarce Rainfall zone is Kurnool + Anantapuramu.
Main soils: deltaic/coastal alluvial, black cotton (regur) and red loamy/sandy.
Land use (2023-24): net sown area about 30.4% (largest); recorded forest about 22.63%; total area about 162.97 lakh ha.
items.source: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 (agro-climatic zones, soils, land use); IMD AP climate profile

items.title: Minerals & Forests (ISFR 2023)
items.body:
**In one line:** AP is so rich in minerals it is nicknamed 'Ratna Garbha', and it also holds important forests, including India's famous second-largest mangroves.

**Why it is asked:** Matching a mineral to its place (barytes-Mangampeta, uranium-Thummalapalli, granite-Chimakurthy) and the ISFR forest figures are standard APPSC items.

## The story

A **mineral** is a useful natural substance dug from the earth. AP has so many that it is called **'Ratna Garbha'** — 'womb of gems'. Its best-known deposits are the **barytes** of **Mangampeta** (YSR Kadapa), among the **largest in the world**; the **uranium** of **Thummalapalli**; and the prized **black granite** of **Chimakurthy** (Prakasam). The long coast adds **heavy mineral beach sands** (such as ilmenite and monazite).

Forests are measured in two different ways, and students often mix them up. **Forest cover** is what satellites actually see as green canopy. **Recorded (notified) forest area** is the land the government has officially marked as forest on paper — it is usually larger, because some marked land has lost its trees.

By the **India State of Forest Report (ISFR) 2023**, AP's **forest cover is 30,084.96 sq km, about 18.46%** of the state, while its **recorded forest area is 37,221.11 sq km, about 22.84%**. **Alluri Sitharama Raju** has the most forest; **Guntur** among the least. AP's **mangroves** (salt-tolerant coastal trees) in the Godavari and Krishna estuaries form India's **second-largest** mangrove stretch after the Sundarbans, protected mainly at **Coringa**.

## Picture it

| Place | Mineral |
|---|---|
| Mangampeta (YSR Kadapa) | Barytes (among world's largest) |
| Thummalapalli (YSR Kadapa) | Uranium |
| Chimakurthy (Prakasam) | Black granite |
| North-coast beaches | Heavy mineral sands |

## Terms explained

- **Mineral** — a useful natural material mined from the ground.
- **Ratna Garbha** — 'womb of gems', AP's nickname for its mineral wealth.
- **Barytes** — a heavy white mineral used in oil-drilling fluids, paint and chemicals.
- **Forest cover** — tree canopy actually seen by satellite.
- **Recorded (notified) forest area** — land legally marked as forest on paper (usually larger than cover).
- **Mangrove** — salt-tolerant trees that grow where river estuaries meet the sea.

## Don't confuse

- **Forest cover (18.46%) is NOT the same as recorded forest area (22.84%)** — one is seen by satellite, the other is a legal paper figure.
- **Barytes is Mangampeta; uranium is Thummalapalli** — do not swap them, even though both are in Kadapa.

## Remember it

Kadapa's twin treasures = **Barytes (Mangampeta) + Uranium (Thummalapalli)**; satellite cover (18.46%) is less than the paper figure (22.84%).

## TL;DR

- AP = 'Ratna Garbha'; minerals include barytes, uranium, black granite, beach sands, limestone, iron ore and diamonds.
- Mangampeta (Kadapa) barytes is among the world's largest; uranium at Thummalapalli; black granite at Chimakurthy.
- ISFR 2023: forest cover 18.46% (30,084.96 sq km) versus recorded forest area 22.84% (37,221.11 sq km).
- AP has India's second-largest mangroves (Godavari and Krishna estuaries; Coringa is the main sanctuary).
keyPoints: AP = 'Ratna Garbha'; minerals include barytes, oil/gas, beach sands, limestone, iron ore, uranium, granite and diamonds.
Mangampeta (YSR Kadapa) is among the world's largest barytes deposits; uranium at Thummalapalli; black granite at Chimakurthy.
ISFR 2023: forest cover 18.46% (30,084.96 sq km) versus recorded/notified forest area 22.84% (37,221.11 sq km) — different concepts.
Alluri Sitharama Raju has AP's largest forest cover; Guntur the least.
AP has India's second-largest mangroves in the Godavari and Krishna estuaries (Coringa).
items.mnemonic: 'Ratna Garbha' barytes king = Mangampeta; forest cover 18.46% < notified 22.84%.
items.source: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 (minerals); ISFR 2023 Vol.2 (AP forests & mangroves)

items.title: Protected Areas, Wetlands, Biodiversity & Hazards
items.body:
**In one line:** AP protects its wildlife through a small set of flagship reserves and wetlands, while its coast and interior face sharp natural hazards — cyclones and floods on one side, drought on the other.

**Why it is asked:** 'NSTR is a tiger reserve', 'Seshachalam is the biosphere reserve', 'Kolleru is the Ramsar site' and 'Hudhud 2014 hit Visakhapatnam' are repeat APPSC facts.

## The story

A **protected area** is land set aside by law to save wildlife. Present-day AP has a compact network: **one Tiger Reserve** — **Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (NSTR)**, about 3,727 sq km and among India's largest, in the Nallamala hills where the **Chenchu** tribe lives; **one Elephant Reserve** — **Rayala (Koundinya)** in Chittoor; **one Biosphere Reserve** — **Seshachalam**, home of the endemic **Red Sanders** tree; plus **three National Parks** (including **Sri Venkateswara** and **Papikonda**) and **13 Wildlife Sanctuaries**.

AP's **wetlands** matter too. **Kolleru Lake**, lying between the Krishna and Godavari deltas, is a large **freshwater** lake and AP's only **Ramsar site** (a wetland of international importance). **Pulicat** is a **brackish** (part-salty) lagoon shared with Tamil Nadu; **Rollapadu** in Kurnool protects the **Great Indian Bustard**.

A **hazard** is a natural event that can cause disaster. The AP coast is among India's **most cyclone-prone**: **Cyclone Hudhud (2014)** devastated Visakhapatnam. The Godavari and Krishna bring **floods** and **storm surges**, and the shore suffers **erosion**. In contrast, **Rayalaseema** repeatedly faces **drought**.

## Picture it

| Protected area | Type |
|---|---|
| Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (NSTR) | Tiger Reserve (among India's largest) |
| Seshachalam | Biosphere Reserve (Red Sanders) |
| Koundinya (Rayala) | Elephant Reserve |
| Kolleru | Ramsar freshwater lake |
| Pulicat | Brackish lagoon (shared with Tamil Nadu) |

## Terms explained

- **Protected area** — land legally set aside to conserve wildlife.
- **Tiger / Elephant / Biosphere Reserve** — different categories of protected land for specific species or whole ecosystems.
- **Ramsar site** — a wetland listed as internationally important; Kolleru is AP's only one.
- **Brackish** — water that is a mix of fresh and salty, as in a coastal lagoon.
- **Hazard** — a natural event (cyclone, flood, drought) that can cause harm.

## Don't confuse

- **NSTR is a Tiger Reserve; Seshachalam is the Biosphere Reserve** — do not swap them.
- **Kolleru is freshwater and Ramsar-listed; Pulicat is brackish and NOT Ramsar-listed.**
- **The old '6 national parks / 21 sanctuaries' count was for undivided AP** and is outdated.

## Remember it

AP's conservation 'ones': **1 tiger reserve (NSTR), 1 elephant reserve, 1 biosphere reserve, 1 Ramsar site (Kolleru).**

## TL;DR

- Present-day AP: 1 Tiger Reserve (NSTR), 1 Elephant Reserve (Rayala/Koundinya), 1 Biosphere Reserve (Seshachalam), 3 National Parks, 13 Sanctuaries.
- Kolleru (freshwater, Ramsar) lies between the Krishna and Godavari deltas; Pulicat is a brackish lagoon shared with Tamil Nadu.
- Rollapadu (Kurnool) conserves the Great Indian Bustard; Coringa protects Godavari-estuary mangroves.
- The coast is highly cyclone-prone (Hudhud 2014 hit Visakhapatnam); floods, storm surge and erosion threaten it, while Rayalaseema faces drought.
keyPoints: Present-day AP: 1 Tiger Reserve (NSTR), 1 Elephant Reserve (Rayala/Koundinya), 1 Biosphere Reserve (Seshachalam), 3 National Parks, 13 Sanctuaries.
Kolleru (freshwater, Ramsar) lies between the Krishna and Godavari deltas; Pulicat is a brackish lagoon shared with Tamil Nadu.
Rollapadu (Kurnool) conserves the Great Indian Bustard; Coringa protects Godavari-estuary mangroves.
AP is in the Deccan Bio-Geographic Zone; endemic Red Sanders; fauna include Golden Gecko, Indian Bison, Great Indian Bustard.
The AP coast is highly cyclone-prone (Hudhud 2014 hit Visakhapatnam); floods, storm surge, coastal erosion and Rayalaseema drought are key hazards.
items.source: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25; AP Protected Areas & Wildlife (2011); disaster records

items.title: Flora, Fauna, Forests & Sanctuaries of Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
**In one line:** AP's forests are mostly dry deciduous, hold the endemic Red Sanders tree and India's second-largest mangroves, and shelter rare animals such as Jerdon's Courser and wild elephants.

**Why it is asked:** 'Red Sanders is endemic to AP', 'Jerdon's Courser only in Sri Lankamalleswara' and 'Koundinya has AP's only wild elephants' are high-frequency APPSC facts.

## The story

**Flora** means plant life; **fauna** means animal life. AP's most widespread forest type is **Southern tropical dry deciduous** — trees that shed their leaves in the dry season. **Teak and bamboo** grow in the Godavari and north-coastal forests.

The star plant is **Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus)**. 'Endemic' means it grows naturally nowhere else; Red Sanders is **endemic** to AP's southern Eastern Ghats (the **Seshachalam-Palakonda-Lankamalla** belt). Because its red wood is so valuable, it is heavily **smuggled** and is protected under CITES. Along the coast, salt-tolerant **mangroves** at **Coringa** form India's **second-largest** mangrove stretch after the Sundarbans.

The animals are just as special. **Jerdon's Courser** is a **critically endangered**, night-active bird found nowhere else on earth except **Sri Lankamalleswara Wildlife Sanctuary** in Kadapa; thought extinct, it was dramatically **rediscovered in 1986**. **Koundinya Wildlife Sanctuary** in Chittoor is AP's **only** home for wild Asian elephants, which wandered in from Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The coast also hosts Indian Bison (Gaur), the Golden Gecko and nesting olive-ridley turtles.

## Picture it

| AP natural 'first' | What / where |
|---|---|
| Red Sanders | Endemic tree, southern Eastern Ghats |
| Coringa | India's 2nd-largest mangrove |
| Jerdon's Courser | Only in Sri Lankamalleswara WLS, Kadapa |
| Koundinya WLS | AP's only wild elephants |

## Terms explained

- **Flora / fauna** — plant life / animal life.
- **Deciduous** — trees that drop their leaves in the dry season.
- **Endemic** — found naturally in one place only, and nowhere else.
- **Critically endangered** — at extremely high risk of extinction.
- **CITES** — the international treaty that controls trade in threatened species (it protects Red Sanders).

## Don't confuse

- **Red Sanders is NOT sandalwood** — sandalwood (Santalum album) is chiefly a Karnataka/Tamil Nadu tree; Red Sanders is the AP endemic.
- **Jerdon's Courser lives only in Sri Lankamalleswara (Kadapa)** — not in NSTR or Coringa.
- **Koundinya, not NSTR, has AP's wild elephants.**

## Remember it

AP's wildlife 'onlys': endemic tree **Red Sanders**, only-habitat bird **Jerdon's Courser**, only-elephants sanctuary **Koundinya**, 2nd mangrove **Coringa**.

## TL;DR

- Southern tropical dry deciduous is AP's most widespread forest type; teak and bamboo occur in Godavari/north-coastal forests.
- Red Sanders is endemic to AP's southern Eastern Ghats (Seshachalam-Palakonda-Lankamalla) and is CITES-protected.
- Coringa (Godavari estuary) is India's second-largest mangrove after the Sundarbans.
- Jerdon's Courser (rediscovered 1986) survives only in Sri Lankamalleswara WLS, Kadapa; Koundinya WLS has AP's only wild elephants.
keyPoints: Southern tropical dry deciduous is AP's most widespread forest type; teak and bamboo occur in Godavari/north-coastal forests.
Red Sanders is endemic to AP's southern Eastern Ghats (Seshachalam-Palakonda-Lankamalla); CITES-protected.
Coringa (Godavari estuary) is India's second-largest mangrove after the Sundarbans.
Present-day AP: 1 tiger reserve (NSTR), 1 biosphere reserve (Seshachalam), national parks Sri Venkateswara and Papikonda.
Jerdon's Courser (rediscovered 1986) survives only in Sri Lankamalleswara WLS, Kadapa.
Koundinya WLS (Chittoor) is AP's only sanctuary with wild Asian elephants; Nelapattu is a major pelican breeding site.
items.mnemonic: AP 'firsts': Red Sanders (endemic tree), Coringa (2nd mangrove), Jerdon's Courser (only-habitat bird), Koundinya (only elephants).

items.title: For Mains — Physical Geography of Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
**In one line:** For Mains (Paper-II, General Studies - geography of India and AP), physical geography is asked not as a list of facts but as a resource-and-hazard story: how AP's relief, rivers, minerals and forests shape its development and its vulnerabilities.

This note serves syllabus clauses **M2-11** (physical features and resources of India and AP) and **M2-14** (fauna and floral geography). Examiners reward answers that convert the Prelims facts into analysis — linking relief to soils to agriculture, and resources to conservation conflict.

## Dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Features | Three belts (coastal plains, Eastern Ghats, Rayalaseema plateau); east-flowing rivers; 974 km coast |
| Significance | Delta rice-bowl, Ratna Garbha minerals, ports, second-largest mangroves |
| Problems | Coast-versus-Rayalaseema water imbalance, cyclones and floods, Red Sanders smuggling, mining in tribal forests |
| Way forward | Inter-basin transfers, mangrove shelter-belts, eco-sensitive-zone rules, community (Chenchu) conservation |

## Data points to quote

- ISFR 2023: forest cover 18.46% (30,084.96 sq km) versus recorded forest area 22.84% (37,221.11 sq km).
- Coastline about 974 km (longest on India's east coast); Visakhapatnam the only major port.
- Mangampeta (Kadapa) barytes among the world's largest; Tummalapalli uranium among the largest reserves.
- Cyclone Hudhud (2014) at Visakhapatnam; Michaung (2023) and Montha (2025) hit the coast — use for disaster-management angle.
- Polavaram National Project (Godavari); Handri-Neeva lift to drought-prone Rayalaseema.

## AP angle

Stress the sharp internal contrast: a water-rich, cyclone-exposed delta coast against a chronically drought-hit Rayalaseema. This single tension explains AP's lift-irrigation push, its disaster-management stakes, and the clash between mining or aquaculture and fragile Eastern-Ghats and estuarine ecosystems.

## Use in answers

- Example: cite Hudhud (2014) and Montha (2025) when arguing for mangrove shelter-belts and early-warning systems.
- Quote: AP as 'Ratna Garbha' (womb of gems) to open a resources answer.
- Diagram idea: a simple west-to-east cross-section (Rayalaseema plateau - Eastern Ghats - coastal delta - Bay of Bengal) instantly shows relief, soils and the water gradient.
keyPoints: Mains (Paper-II, clauses M2-11 and M2-14) asks physical geography as a resource-and-hazard story, not a fact list.
Frame answers along features, significance, problems and way forward; link relief to soils to agriculture.
Quote ISFR 2023 (cover 18.46% versus recorded 22.84%), 974 km coast, Mangampeta barytes, Tummalapalli uranium, Polavaram.
Core AP angle: water-rich cyclone-prone delta coast versus drought-prone Rayalaseema, driving lift irrigation and disaster management.
Use recent cyclones (Hudhud 2014, Montha 2025), the 'Ratna Garbha' quote, and a west-to-east cross-section diagram.
